newsitem.title: UK: British bosses upbeat on business prospects.
newsitem.headline: British bosses upbeat on business prospects.

text.p: Financial bosses at top British companies are more positive now about their business prospects than at any corresponding time in the 1990s, according to a survey published on Saturday.
The survey, which received the views of more than 200 finance directors and corporate treasurers, was compiled by market research group Consensus Research International.
"Top finanancial executives in the UK's largest public companies enter 1997 in a more positive frame of mind than in any of our earlier surveys in the 1990s," it said.
The survey found that 84 percent expressed "some degree of optimism" with 22 percent reporting they were "very optimistic" about their own companies' prospects for the year ahead.
Just over 60 percent were optimistic for their sector, with a similar number upbeat about British industry as a whole.

"These levels of optimism are tempered slightly by an expectation of slightly less favourable economic conditions over the next three years. Interest rates and inflation are both expected...to be higher -- albeit only slightly so," it added.
Any improvement in the rate of economic growth is expected to be marginal. "It may be, therefore, that 1997 is perceived to be the top of the business cycle", the report said.

It also found that the "overwhelming balance of opinion (81 percent) is that there will be a Labour government in power after the general election" and that only 12 percent predicted a Conservative victory. Only seven percent did not respond.
Britain's Conservative government must call an election by May.

The main corporate priorities over the next three years will be the development of new markets, cited by 47 percent, reduction of the cost base, cited by 41 percent, and change in organisational structure, 40 percent.

Key issues companies say they will be trying to focus on in their investor relations programmes are "improved differentiation (47 percent), building their corporate image (45 percent) and how they are developing new markets (40 percent)", the survey found.
